posts.name: Abdulqoyyum Olamide Aileru
posts.cooked:
1. Project Overview

  • Project name: ShareCut
  • One-sentence summary: promoters get a personal QR code for a shop; when a customer they referred buys, the shop’s Fiber node pays the promoter’s cut automatically, at most once per sale, and both payments appear on a public receipts page.
  • Project type: a public web MVP anyone can try from a browser, a payout service, a failure lab, and a 14-day field pilot in 3 Lagos shops (testnet)
  • Funding requested: $713, paid in CKB ($600 for technical milestones, $113 direct costs; see section 7)
  • Duration: 7 weeks

Revision (v2): following the committee’s feedback:

  1. The pilot now has pre-registered hypotheses with pass/fail thresholds and a decision rule (section 4).
  2. The budget no longer uses an hourly rate: technical work is priced per milestone, and the direct costs of the pilot are listed separately (section 7).
  3. A public web MVP that anyone can join from a browser now goes live in week 2, before the field pilot.

ShareCut is a production-side Fiber app: it gives shops a reason to create payments (one sale, one payout) instead of adding another way to pay.

2. Team Profile

Abdul (solo), software engineer, Lagos, Nigeria. Student at the University of Lagos.

  • About 5 years of experience. Senior Software Engineer at Go Digital Africa, where I led SNBS and co-led Linkly.
  • LLM evaluation work at Celsius; Paystack payment integrations; designed a Stellar/Soroban USDC escrow dApp for a bounty.
  • I write Rust and TypeScript.
  • New to CKB and Fiber. Anything that breaks on FNN gets written up and filed upstream, not patched in private.

GitHub: github.com/Olagold-hackxx · Repo: github.com/Olagold-hackxx/sharecut · LinkedIn: www.linkedin.com/in/abdulqoyyum-aileru-017b75253 · Discord: olagoldhackxx · Email: aileruenterprise@gmail.com

3. Project Background

Why I want to build this. Most of what I’ve built so far has been payments: Paystack integrations at work, and an escrow app on Stellar. The problem I keep running into, though, isn’t paying. It’s getting customers. Small businesses around me in Lagos live on word of mouth, and the people who bring in customers usually get nothing, or a “thank you, I’ll sort you out later” that never comes. I want to see whether paying them automatically, per sale, changes anything. Fiber is a good place to try it because tiny, frequent payments are its whole point.

The everyday problem. The shops I have in mind are the ordinary ones near campus and in the markets: provisions, food, printing, phone accessories. Their marketing is mostly WhatsApp statuses and people telling their friends. Rewarding the people who bring customers is done three ways today, and each one leaks:

How it’s done today What goes wrong
Cash or a transfer “when I see you” Forgotten, uneven, no record of who sent whom
A discount for the customer The promoter gets nothing, so they stop sending people
Nothing at all The owner can’t tell which promoters actually bring sales

I haven’t measured this yet. Before the pilot I’ll talk to the 3 pilot owners and post what they said in the first weekly update, including anything that contradicts this table.

Existing work, and what this reuses.

  • FNN (github.com/nervosnetwork/fiber), latest release pinned at kickoff, unpatched.
  • The official browser WASM / fiber-js node for promoters, not a custom one.
  • FiberFlow (github.com/Ticoworld/fiberflow) for checkout invoices and events. I haven’t tested it yet. Week 1 decides between FiberFlow’s events and polling get_invoice directly, and the decision is written in FIBER_NOTES.md.
  • Fiber Link’s hosted-node pattern as the fallback for promoters who can’t keep a browser node online.

What’s new: attribution of each sale to a promoter, an exactly-once payout service, a payout queue for promoters who are offline, and a public receipts page that links every payout to the sale that caused it. I found no existing referral-payout tool for Fiber; if one exists, I’ll build on it instead.

Why Fiber, and when it isn’t needed. In Nigeria, OPay and Moniepoint already make transfers cheap and instant, so cost isn’t the argument. Fiber lets a shop pay many small amounts automatically, tied to each sale, to promoters who only need a Fiber node, not bank details. If owners are happy tracking referrals in a notebook and paying by transfer, ShareCut isn’t needed. H4 below tests exactly that.

4. Solution

Public web MVP (anyone, anywhere, from week 2):

  1. Open the demo link posted on this thread. The demo shop page starts.
  2. Open the promoter page in a second browser or phone. It starts the official browser Fiber node and creates your promoter QR.
  3. Get testnet CKB from the faucet and pay a test sale through your promoter link.
  4. Watch your promoter cut arrive on the promoter page, and see the sale and payout side by side on the public receipts page.
  5. Close the promoter tab, make another sale, and reopen it: the queued payout arrives.

Field pilot (3 shops near UNILAG, 14 days, weeks 5–6):

  1. Each shop gets a counter QR, and 3–4 promoters each get a personal QR card (10 promoters in total).
  2. Customers pay the shop the normal way (cash or transfer), because they can’t pay with test CKB.
  3. When a referred customer buys, the shop scans the promoter’s QR on a phone and enters the amount. The shop’s node pays a testnet Fiber invoice that mirrors the sale, and the payout service pays the promoter’s 5% cut.
  4. Owners and promoters see every sale and payout on the receipts page.

Pre-registered hypotheses. Posted on this thread before week 1. Anyone may add a failure scenario, and I commit to running what is added.

# Hypothesis Pass if If it fails, the report publishes
H1 Payouts are exactly-once 0 double payouts and 0 missed payouts across 6 failure scenarios × 3 runs, and across the whole pilot Which scenario broke it, how many payouts were affected, and the fix
H2 Offline promoters still get paid ≥ 90% of queued payouts delivered within 24 h of the promoter’s node coming back online Delivery times, and whether the hosted-node fallback was needed
H3 It fits a real counter Median time to log a referred sale < 30 s; ≥ 2 of 3 shops still logging in week 2 Times, drop-off point, and what owners said
H4 Recorded, automatic payouts get promoters referring ≥ 20 referred sales in 14 days and ≥ 6 of 10 promoters with at least 1 sale Real counts. If promoters don’t refer, the report says a notebook and a transfer are enough

Decision rule: if H1–H4 pass, I’ll keep building and look at mainnet once a stable-value route exists. If H4 fails, I’ll report it as a negative result and stop.

What this pilot does not claim. Pilot payments are testnet CKB mirroring real cash sales, and the project pays the mobile data. The pilot measures reliability, attribution and fit with a real shop’s routine. It makes no claim about demand for real-money payouts.

5. Technical Architecture

Shop node (VPS): FNN native node, release pinned at kickoff. Browser nodes connect to it over WebSocket.

Payout service (Rust):

  1. A sale creates an invoice with new_invoice. The service stores payment_hash → promoter_id, amount before the invoice is shown.
  2. The service watches the invoice (FiberFlow events, or polling get_invoice until the status is Paid).
  3. On Paid, it writes a payout record keyed by the sale’s payment_hash with status pending. A unique key on that hash means a second event for the same sale can’t create a second payout.
  4. It sends the cut with send_payment (keysend: true, target_pubkey = the promoter’s node), putting the sale’s payment_hash in custom_records so each payout carries a reference to its sale.
  5. It checks the result with get_payment and marks the record sent or failed. Failed or offline payouts stay queued and are retried with backoff. Before any retry, the service checks list_payments so a payout that actually went through is never sent twice.

Promoter page: runs the official WASM / fiber-js node. On first visit it calls connect_peer to the shop node, and the shop node opens a channel to the promoter with open_channel (public: false, one_way: true), funded with testnet CKB, since the channel only ever pays the promoter. If a promoter’s browser can’t stay reachable, the fallback is a hosted node account (custodial), and the report counts how many promoters needed it.

Shop counter page: a mobile web page to scan a promoter QR, enter the sale amount and pay the mirrored invoice from the shop’s node.

Receipts page: lists every sale and payout with payment hashes, timings and status. Promoter and device IDs are hashed. Logs are append-only JSON and published at the end.

Failure lab (week 3), 6 scenarios × 3 runs:

  1. The same Paid event delivered twice
  2. The payout service crashes between writing the record and sending
  3. The shop’s node restarts mid-payout
  4. The promoter’s tab is closed when a payout is due
  5. The promoter’s channel runs out of balance
  6. The sale invoice expires before it’s paid

Hard parts, which are the point of the test: promoters’ browser nodes go offline when phones lock or tabs close; Lagos 4G drops; and an exactly-once guarantee has to survive crashes, not just the happy path.

Out of scope: mainnet, real money, stablecoins, fiat cash-out, multi-shop accounts, any business or go-to-market work.

6. Weekly Execution Plan (7 weeks, about 10 hours a week)

Week Focus Concrete output
1 FNN on the VPS; test FiberFlow events vs polling get_invoice; test keysend with custom_records to a browser node First testnet payment hashes; decisions written in FIBER_NOTES.md
2 Public web MVP: demo shop, promoter page, receipts page Demo link posted on this thread; anyone can try it; tag v0.1; hypotheses and scenarios posted
3 Payout service hardening and failure lab Scenario table with payment hashes and outcomes for all 18 runs
4 Shop counter page; print QR materials; onboard 3 shops and 10 promoters Owners and promoters confirm on this thread before week 5; printer receipt posted
5–6 14-day field pilot; public MVP stays open Daily log export; mid-pilot numbers in the weekly update
7 Interviews, report, reproducibility Report with H1–H4 results; logs published; closing post on this thread

If fewer than 3 shops or 10 promoters confirm, the report states the real numbers as a result.

7. Funding Requirements: $713 in CKB

Technical work is priced as a fixed amount per milestone, not an hourly rate. The direct costs of running and verifying the pilot are listed separately. If the committee prefers direct costs only, the milestone lines come out and the $113 in direct costs stands.

Technical milestones ($600)

Weeks Work USD
1 to 2 Public web MVP: demo shop, promoter page with the browser Fiber node, receipts page; tag v0.1 300
3 Exactly-once payout service and payout queue; failure lab, 6 scenarios × 3 runs, published 200
4 Shop counter page and pilot setup 100

Direct costs ($113)

Item Basis USD
VPS for the FNN node, payout service and receipts page DigitalOcean Basic, 2 GB, $12/month × 3 months (build, pilot, and 30 days of demo after the report) 36
Pilot materials 3 counter QR stands, 30 promoter QR cards, 3 A4 posters (estimate; printer’s receipt published) 25
Mobile data during the pilot 3 owners + 10 promoters × about $2 for 14 days (estimate; receipts published) 26
Feedback interviews Airtime thank-you for each of the 13 participants who completes the end-of-pilot interview, about $2 each (estimate) 26
Testnet transaction and channel fees Testnet CKB comes free from the faucet, so there’s nothing to sponsor 0

Total: $713 ($600 technical milestones + $113 direct costs)

20% at launch ($142.60). The remaining 80% ($570.40) on completion against the deliverables in section 8. Fund usage is disclosed at completion against these tables, and any unspent direct-cost money goes back.

8. Deliverables and Verification

None of these checks need a code review.

Deliverable How to verify
Public web MVP Open the demo link from this thread, get testnet CKB from the faucet, pay a test sale through your own promoter link, and watch your cut arrive
Offline payout Close your promoter tab, make a sale, reopen it: the queued payout arrives and shows on the receipts page
Receipts page Every sale listed next to its payout, with payment hashes and timings
Failure lab The scenario table lists all 18 runs with payment hashes; anyone can re-run a scenario from the README
Field pilot (H1–H4) Published logs rebuild every number in the report
Independent participants Owners’ and promoters’ confirmation replies on this thread, dated before week 5
FNN notes FIBER_NOTES.md lists each bug or gap found, each linked to an upstream issue

9. Current State vs. Funded Scope

Already exists (not funded): the public repo with a README and MIT licence.

Funded by this grant: the public web MVP, payout service, failure lab and shop counter page (the section 7 milestones), plus the server and pilot costs for the 14-day field pilot.

Explicitly out of scope: mainnet, real-money payouts or a stablecoin, fiat cash-out, business or go-to-market work.

10. CKB Ecosystem Alignment

  • Production-side Fiber app: every referred sale creates a payment and a payout. It isn’t another checkout or payment entry point.
  • Anyone can verify it: the public web MVP works from any browser, and the receipts page shows every payment.
  • Reuses before building: FNN unpatched, the official WASM / fiber-js node, FiberFlow if its events fit, and Fiber Link’s hosted-node pattern as the fallback.
  • Evidence for open questions: browser nodes that go offline and must still receive payments, under real conditions.
  • Honest limit: testnet only. With USDI’s operator ceasing operations there is no public mainnet stable-value route. The report records what a mainnet version would need, without claiming it.

How it differs from nearby projects:

  • Dular covers mobile payments and cashing out to fiat. ShareCut doesn’t touch fiat.
  • Fiber Link is tipping between users. ShareCut payouts are tied to a specific sale and set by the shop.

Risks and Mitigations

Risk Mitigation
Fewer than 3 shops or 10 promoters join Recruit 4 shops and 12 promoters before week 5; if still short, report the real count
A pilot shop drops out A named backup shop confirms on this thread before week 5
Promoters’ browser nodes are rarely online That is H2 data; the hosted-node fallback is ready, and the report counts who needed it
Owners find logging at the counter too slow That is H3 data; the counter page is a single scan plus an amount
FNN or WASM bug blocks the flow Pin the release, file the issue upstream, document the workaround in FIBER_NOTES.md
Participants confuse test CKB with real money Every page and QR card says “testnet, no real money”; payouts in naira stay whatever the shop already does

posts.name: 行天春彦
posts.cooked:
Hi @abdul,

Thank you for your continued interest in the Spark Program and for submitting the ShareCut proposal.

After review by the Spark Program committee, your proposal’s status is Pending. This is not a rejection, but an invitation to revise your proposal.

Two questions the committee is concerned about:

Clarify the expected outcomes of the rollout: The proposal mentions piloting the program at at least two brick-and-mortar shops, but does not specify what results or tangible progress would count as success. Please provide concrete expectations for the pilot, such as the number of promoters per shop, the number of referred customers or payment transactions you expect to generate, and the metrics you will use to determine whether this idea merits further development. The committee needs measurable goals to evaluate the pilot’s results.

Revise the budget structure: The current budget appears to use a calculation method that is inconsistent with Spark’s principles. Spark funds expenses required by the project, not the time of community members. Please revise the budget to list actual necessary expenses, such as testnet node operating costs, promotional materials for pilot stores (QR codes, flyers), sponsored transaction fees for pilot participants, and other direct costs. Development work itself is not an eligible Spark budget item.

Please revise and resubmit your proposal based on this feedback. We’ll arrange another review as soon as possible.

If you have questions about the budget structure or need help connecting with Fiber-related resources, feel free to contact us anytime—the committee will be happy to help.

Best regards
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee

posts.name: Abdulqoyyum Olamide Aileru
posts.cooked:
Hi @xingtian, thanks for the feedback. I’ve revised the proposal:

  1. Pilot outcomes: added four pre-registered hypotheses with pass/fail thresholds and a rule for continuing or stopping:

    • payouts happen exactly once
    • promoters still get paid when their browser was offline
    • logging a sale fits a real shop counter
    • promoters actually bring customers (at least 20 referred sales and 6 of 10 promoters with a sale in 14 days)

    A public web demo anyone can try also goes live in week 2.

  2. Budget: removed development time. It now lists only direct costs, $113 in total: the VPS, QR and print materials for the pilot shops, mobile data for participants, and airtime for feedback interviews. Testnet fees are $0 because test CKB comes from the faucet.

Thanks again, and happy to adjust anything else.

posts.name: Abdulqoyyum Olamide Aileru
posts.cooked:
Hi @xingtian, one question on the budget so I get it right.

The Spark guidelines list technical development (prototype building) as an eligible use, so I’ve updated section 7: the technical deliverables (public web demo, payout service and failure tests, shop counter page) are now priced as fixed amounts per milestone, not an hourly rate, with the direct pilot costs listed separately. The total is $713 ($600 milestones + $113 direct costs).

Could you confirm whether that structure is acceptable? If the committee prefers direct costs only, I’ll remove the milestone lines and the $113 stands.

Thanks!

posts.name: 行天春彦
posts.cooked:
Hi @abdul,

Thank you for taking the time to revise the proposal based on our earlier feedback.

After review by the Spark Program committee, your proposal still assigned a status of Pending.

Main Revision Recommendations:

  1. Deliverables: The current deliverables only contain the confirmation replies from the shop owner and promoter in the post. This falls short of the final report format the committee previously endorsed. Please clarify what constitutes the final deliverable and align it with the committee-recognized report structure.

  2. Budget Calculation: The current budget calculation method still has issues. Please review the cost breakdown and clearly distinguish the budget for technical milestones from direct costs to avoid double counting. The milestones in the current budget form are divided by timeline rather than by deliverables. As a result, the milestone budget and hard-cost budget partially overlap, making verification more complex. Please reorganize the current budget using either deliverable-based milestones or hard costs, rather than mixing the two approaches.

Please revise and resubmit based on the feedback above. We will arrange a new round of review as soon as possible.

Best,
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee
